entries.title: I Put on Meta and Xreal’s XR Glasses. Face Computers Are Finally Getting Good
entries.summary: Xreal’s long-hyped Aura glasses arrive soon for $1,279. Here’s how they fare against Meta’s recently announced VR Glasses.
entries.content:
I’m sorry to say, but the $1,299 Meta VR Glasses might just be very good.

That's despite the company's well-earned flak over privacy issues with its smart glasses and the general uneasiness people feel about being recorded. But in the 30 to 45 minutes or so I spent wearing the mixed-reality glasses at Meta’s Connect event in September, I was astounded by the video quality and wearability of a device that has for so long come in the form of a heavy, hot headset.

But it’s not the only big dog in the face computer world. Not by a long shot. Xreal, known for its virtual-display glasses, has partnered with Google to build mixed-reality smart glasses on the Android XR platform—the Xreal Aura. On Wednesday, the company announced the official price, starting at $1,279. That’s 20 bucks cheaper than Meta’s VR glasses. Unlike Meta’s option, the Aura glasses come out this year.

The Auras are available for preorder, but only for people who have already placed paid reservations. Preorder options will open up for the general public “in the coming weeks.” The starting price is for a model with 12 GB of RAM and 256 GB storage. Xreal says units will ship in the US, Canada, Japan, and South Korea. It will launch in more regions in 2027.

I tried both. I attended a demo of the Aura glasses, which was deliberately held a day after Meta announced its VR Glasses at Meta Connect. My immediate takeaway was that these glasses are direct competitors, with very similar experiences. Put on a pair, and you can watch videos, play games, or project a multi-monitor workplace setup. Some of those experiences work better on one device or the other.

Same but Different

Smart glasses come in several varieties. The simple ones plug into your phone or laptop and project the screen onto the glasses, acting like a portable monitor that doesn’t require you to crane your neck. Then there are glasses like the Ray-Ban Meta, which feature a camera to capture photos and videos and an AI assistant you can talk to. Display versions of these glasses—and ones coming from Google and Samsung—add a visual component so you can see real-time captions when people speak, translations, navigation instructions, and more.

But mixed reality glasses go a step further, bridging the world of virtual and augmented reality. They’re more akin to headsets like the Apple Vision Pro or the Meta Quest, but in slimmer, lighter designs that aren’t as cumbersome to wear. Snap also recently announced a competing pair called Specs, which cost $2,195 and are shipping later this year.

Neither Meta nor Xreal’s glasses can be mistaken for regular everyday glasses. Meta’s futuristic frames fit like the front half of a VR headset. The Xreal frames are more glasses-forward; chunky but nowhere near as thicc as Snap's Specs. Both have an attached wired compute puck (the thing that houses all the memory and processing power) that you'll need to put in your pocket.

On the Meta VR Glasses, the interactive experiences feel smooth and fluid. The glasses can run all the services that already exist on Meta’s Quest devices on a gorgeous 5K micro-OLED screen. They also have more cameras. (Two point straight down at your lap, so you should probably keep pants on when using these things.) That enables hand tracking features that feel very precise. Typing sentences out on a virtual keyboard feels almost seamless. On Xreal’s glasses, it feels more like hunting and pecking.

The Xreal Aura glasses generally feel less polished. The glasses can run anything built in Android. That works most of the time, but in my demo it also led to some apps not syncing right. Android is a huge platform, and not everything will adapt to mixed reality.

What you can do in the Aura much better than Meta’s VR Glasses is walk around. The Aura has lenses with real-world passthrough, meaning when you turn the screen off, it’s like looking through a regular pair of glasses. Meta’s VR Glasses have video passthrough, which can look fuzzy.

Ultimately, the Meta VR Glasses feel better for sitting and experiencing content, or typing something out. But the Xreal Aura adapts to the real world better—or at least makes it easier to see what’s in front of you while you’re walking around.

Meta’s glasses launch early next year, so we’ll have a clearer verdict once we get extensive time with the final hardware.

entries.title: Save Up to 44% With the 18 Best Prime Day Toy Deals (2026)
entries.summary: Snag some gifts for your kiddos or unleash your inner child with the best Prime Day toy deals, including Lego, STEM toys, and board games.
entries.content:
Whether you need a birthday gift, you’re looking ahead to the holidays, or your little ones simply deserve a treat, these are the best Prime Day toy deals this year.

I’ve been buying too many toys, board games, and Lego sets for my kids for many, many years. I’m not afraid to admit I still love playing with toys either. In fact, a lot of Lego sets are now aimed at adults who grew up with it (and have the disposable income). Everything here has been built, played with, and thoroughly tested by my family, and most have been tried out in a classroom full of kids (my wife is a teacher).

You should also check out our roundup of the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals.

Updated on October 7 at 7:30 am ET: Added some new STEM toy deals and checked through the current products on sale.

WIRED Featured Deals

  • A screen-free kid's sound stage: Qubs Qubitunes for $73 ($53 off)
  • A marble run maze puzzle: ThinkFun Gravity Maze for $16 ($9 off)
  • A fun family board game: Azul for $24 ($16 off)
  • A smart Star Wars Lego set: Smart Play Throne Room Duel and A-Wing for $128 ($32 off)

Best Prime Day Toy Deals

This screen-free play stage and speaker for kids is great fun. Slot a wooden cartridge in the top and pop wooden character pieces on the circular soundstage, divided into four sections, to change the audio it plays. This basic functionality allows for a clever variety of themed add-on packs, including classical music and a cooking game.

Musical kids aged 3 years and up can start learning with this mini guitar. It's just like a real guitar, only smaller, and with just three strings. The companion Loog app and included lessons are enough to get them started.

These slightly squishy plus-shaped building blocks are satisfying to stick together and pull apart. Every piece is the same shape, so kids don’t have to spend ages searching for a specific block, they can pick by color or build randomly. You can create bracelets and headbands or construct robots and bridges.

The tough, translucent Magna-Tiles click together easily to form two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects. Kids love building houses, castles, vehicles, and whatever else occurs to them with these triangular and square magnetic tiles. We love them so much that they made our best STEM toys guide. The classic set is a fantastic place to start, but be warned: There are themed sets, and you will end up buying more!

Combing the fun of marble runs with maze construction and logic puzzles was a seriously bright idea. Kids of various ages (8 years and up) love building 3D mazes and dropping marbles in the top to see where they emerge. The 60 challenge cards get tougher as you go.

A fantastic gift for kids of all ages, this clever construction kit features Clixo’s colorful, versatile, magnetic pieces that snap together, so you can build three-dimensional shapes, from crowns to cats. The durable and washable pieces stack neatly and pack away easily, and you can play with them anywhere—no table required.

Made from a dozen magnetic shapes, this cube can be reconfigured in a surprising variety of ways. The exteriors are covered in holographic stickers that catch the light, and there’s a spinner accessory and a companion mobile app with building suggestions (though it’s not really necessary). This is irresistible fidgeting fun for anyone.

Miniature mechanics in the making will love this 175-piece kit that can be assembled into a working four-cylinder engine. It's fun but fiddly, so younger kids will need help (age 10 years and up is about right). Just be aware you need three AA batteries (not included) to start it when constructed, so the pistons and gears move and the LEDs light up.

Best Prime Day Board Game Deals

This immersive strategy game is all about gathering and trading resources to build roads, settlements, and cities on a randomly generated board of hexagonal tiles. To collect enough points for a victory requires the right strategy and some luck with dice rolls. My kids love the trading and the robber mechanic, which allows you to steal cards from your opponents and block their resources (though it can cause fall outs). The game is perfect for three or four players and usually lasts around an hour.

In Azul, you must make mosaics by matching tiles with different patterns and colors to get the maximum possible score. Azul is easy to grasp but supports many different tactical approaches and has surprising depth, making it one of the best family board games. The tiles and other components are high quality, and filling your board is deeply satisfying. Play moves quickly, and you can complete a game in less than an hour, but you will want to play again.

Collect sets of super cute sushi cards to match the menu and score points in this compelling and easy to grasp card game. Choose a card each turn to build the best meal and pass on the rest of your hand to the next player. It's quick and fun, but has real strategic depth.

A firm WIRED favorite, Ticket to Ride features steam engine styling and rules that are easy to grasp. All you must do is claim railway routes across the US and Canada using your colorful plastic rail cars. Spend cards to claim routes, rack up bonus points for connecting specific destinations, and the person with the highest score at the end wins. All aboard, choo, choo!

We regularly play this family favorite with visitors because it’s so fun, works for up to eight players, and is very easy to grasp. Each round is based on a single word from a category card determined by a dice roll, and while everyone else knows the word, the chameleon has to bluff their way through. Every player says something associated with the word for that round, and the guesser has to pick out the chameleon.

Somewhere between a board game and a logic puzzle, the Rush Hour series is all about navigating your red car through traffic. There are 120 challenges that get increasingly difficult, and kids will have to carefully consider how to slide the other cars and trucks aside to reach the exit on the grid.

Best Prime Day Lego Deals

Not all of the best gifts for Lego lovers are Lego sets. This handy guide book helps you turn your Lego collection into all kinds of builds. As long as you have a decent number of basic bricks from a dragon to a rescue helicopter with these clear step-by-step instructions.

This fun build lets you reenact the dramatic conclusion of Return of the Jedi, with Darth Vader and Luke Skywalker dueling as Emperor Palpatine looks on and a space battle rages outside. Part of Lego’s new Smart Play system, Smart Bricks light up, and add lightsaber noises, lasers, explosions, heavy breathing, and even a rendition of “The Imperial March.” It’s an expensive set for what you get, but this is first decent discount we’ve seen on it.

Any racing fans will appreciate the Speed Champions McLaren F1 Team MCL38 Race Car Toy, and this is the lowest price I've ever seen for it. This fun build for kids aged 10 years and up includes a minifigure and a McLaren F1 car with a halo bar, rear wing, sponsor stickers, and wider rear tires bearing the “Pirelli” name.

Forget cheap chocolate, most kids (me included) would prefer a Lego Star Wars Advent Calendar, and this year’s one is on sale. It features Mando and Grogu in Christmas jumpers, and each day reveals an ingenious tiny build from creatures like a Bantha or Mudhorn to the Razor Crest ship and an Imperial Shuttle.

entries.title: I Found the 25 Best Prime Day Tech and Gadget Deals (October 2026)
entries.summary: Never pay full price. Bag yourself some Prime Day tech deals on our favorite WIRED-tested gadgets.
entries.content:
Amazon’s Prime Day tech deals are here again. Yes, already. The economy is tough right now, and if you’re feeling this cost-of-living crisis, you probably don’t need that shiny new thing. But if you do need it, you certainly won’t want to pay full price. We put two pieces of research together for you: we track prices to make sure deals are actually deals and we only recommend stuff we believe is worth buying. Seriously: all the Prime Day tech deals you see here have been life-tested by the WIRED Reviews team in our own homes, often using our own families as guinea pigs.

If you haven’t found the deal you want yet, browse our roundup of the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals.

Updated on October 7 at 6:30 am ET: Added some new tech deals and checked through the current products on sale.

  • Nothing’s Best Headphones: Nothing Headphone (1) for $189 ($110 Off)
  • Samsung’s Most Powerful Smartphone: Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra for $980 ($420 Off)
  • Apple’s Rarely Discounted MacBook: Apple MacBook Air for $1,099 ($200 Off)
  • Eufy's Pan-and-Tilt Security Camera: Eufy EufyCam S4 Security Camera for $260 ($90 Off)

Audio and TV Deals

The flagship Apple AirPods Pro 3 are its best wireless earbuds, and they're at the lowest price since June. Music sounds great, noise cancellation works well, and they offer excellent call quality. Apple added more ear tips for a better fit for small ears, new tools like heart rate sensing and live translation, and enhanced support for folks with hearing loss. If you use an iPhone, these are the wireless earbuds for you.

The Nothing Headphone (1) is one of our favorite pairs of over-ear headphones. With an attractive and distinctive design that combines a transparent look with tactile controls like a volume wheel and media control paddle, these headphones make a real statement. They also boast top-notch battery life. This is the best discount we’ve seen on them so far.

Prime Day is a great time to pick up older models at deep discounts. The Sonos Beam Gen 2 is a great example, having coming out originally in 2021. It's since been supplanted by the Sonos Beam Ultra, but that model is hundreds of dollars more (even while on sale!), and the Sonos Beam Gen 2 has never been cheaper. Our own audio expert, Harry Rabinowitz, used this model in his own home as his primary soundbar and found it to be a particularly good fit for smaller homes.

Speaking of deals on older models, if you've always fancied one of those picture-style TVs, this 2025 Samsung model has a matte finish to make paintings and photos look more real, for when you're not using it as a TV. The magnetic bezels are customizable, and some folks love the look. To be honest, these aren't best TVs, sadly, Amazon doesn't have any Prime Day deals on them.

Phones, Wearables, and Accessories Deals

Available in dazzling hibiscus, the Google Pixel 11 stands out, and also happens to be the best option in Google’s new lineup for most people. It boasts an excellent camera, long battery life, and decent performance, alongside Qi2 25W support for magnetic charging and accessories, and super slick contextual AI features.

The Samsung S26 Ultra was the pick of the bunch this year, with a cool privacy screen, blazing performance, long battery life, and an excellent camera, but all three of Samsung’s S26 phones are on sale right now. These are the lowest prices they’ve been so far.

The Moto G Stylus is our pick of the best cheap phones under $400, and is is as low as it has ever been right now. If you miss a headphone jack and microSD card slot, this could be a winner. This is the 2025 model, but Motorola increased the price by $100 for the 2026 Moto G Stylus, and, apart from the upgraded active stylus, there’s little to justify the extra cost.

The Google Pixel Watch 5 is the best smartwatch for Android phone owners. It tracks your activity, sleep, heart rate, and more automatically, and works seamlessly with Gemini. You can also get insights and coaching from Google Health if you subscribe.

This is a solid smartwatch, and an especially great choice if you have a Samsung Galaxy phone. You can save yourself a significant sum by opting for last year’s model and Samsung’s Galaxy Watch9 is only a modest upgrade over the Watch8, considering it’s $120 more expensive.

Anyone with a trio of Apple gadgets (iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods) will benefit from snagging one of the best Apple 3-in-1 wireless chargers for their nightstand, and this is my top pick. The wide base keeps it steady, enabling you to remove your iPhone from the magnetic wireless charging pad one-handed, the Watch pad lets any strap dangle, and the base has a spot for AirPods, too.

This power bank does it all. I love the translucent design, offering a peek at the electronic innards. It has a handy display with comprehensive stats, and it supports just about every fast charging protocol going. It packs 24,000 mAh of power and can charge at up to 140 watts, so it will juice up anything from a laptop down. It’s even IP66 rated for water and dust resistance.

Want a hard-wearing, fast charging cable to keep your gadgetry juiced? This Anker cable from the best USB-C cables is our pick. It can deliver 240 watts, has a tough, braided nylon exterior made from 100 percent recycled plastic, and comes with a lifetime warranty. Anker promises this cable will last a century and it can operate in temperatures from -40 degrees to 176 degrees Fahrenheit. The ribbed cuffs make it easy to grip, and it’s USB-IF certified, too.

Computers and Home Office Deals

The M5 MacBook Air got a serious price hike at the end of June, bringing it up to $1,299. But this week, everyone’s favorite laptop dropped to $1,099, which is the lowest price it’s been at in months. It comes with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage, so you’re getting a really solid configuration that should last you many years. The 15-inch model is also $200 off if you need a larger screen to work on. Regardless, this is the best laptop can buy at the price price I’ve seen it at in a while.

Interesting in dipping your toe in the world of local, agentic AI? I know that will sound cringey to some—and trust me, I get it. But there's no denying the increasing interest in using the Mac Mini for just that, and the latest M6 is particularly good at it, as I learned in my own testing. Of course, the M6 Mac Mini has a broader appeal too, and it's great to see it on sale so soon after launching. If you need even more performance for your AI curiosity, you'll need the Mac Studio, which also received its first discount since launching, coming in at $150 under its retail price.

Gaming laptops have gotten far too expensive recently, so I was delighted to see that one of my favorite gaming laptops to recommend has a huge sale. The price on this has fluctuated wildly over the past few months, but never has it dropped to just $1,100. This is the model that comes with the entry-level RTX 5050, but it has a better display than every other gaming laptop in this price range. Also consider the RTX 5060 model for $1,499 at Walmart, which really takes performance to the next level.

If you don’t want another subscription in your life, the Asus ZenWiFi BT10 is the best mesh system for you. You get three bands of stable Wi-Fi 7 coverage for your home. A two-pack will cover most properties (up to 6,000 square feet), there are two high-speed 10 Gbps ports (alongside a Gigabit LAN and USB 3.0), and security software, parental controls, and extras like VPN support are included. Clip the coupon for the lowest price here.

You won't find a better cheap monitor than this. That's always true of the Dell 27 Plus S2725HSM, but it's especially true at $130, which is the cheapest I've ever seen it at. It's just a basic 1920 x 1080 resolution, but the fully adjustable stand and great image quality gives this a major step up over every comparable monitor I've seen. If you've got some more cash to spend, I'd also recommend the upgraded 4K model, which is also on sale at a new low price.

A tidy, affordable pair of PC speakers, Edifier’s M60 is a bargain at its usual price, so this discount is not to be sniffed at. These speakers produce a surprisingly rich, clear sound that persists when you crank the volume, and there’s a thump of bass. They also come with angled stands, and connect via USB-C, 3.5 mm, or Bluetooth 5.3.

Tablets and E-Reader Deals

The best iPad for most people, if you don’t already have the iPad (11th-generation, A16), now is the time to buy. The 11-inch screen is perfect for kicking back on the couch with a book, game, or movie. It has a pair of 12-megapixel cameras, and Touch ID in the power button. It’s also handy for keeping the kids amused.

Fancy an e-reader that can also serve as a digital notebook? Amazon’s third-generation Kindle Scribe has you covered. It’s slim, with an 11-inch screen, smart stylus, and a bunch of AI features. It’s a go-to choice for note-takers and students. While we recommend the older model in our best Kindles guide, that’s mainly due to the lower price, and this is a better option when it’s on sale. Such as right now.

Home Tech Deals

If you’re looking for an easy security system and you don’t mind paying a pricey subscription ($10 per month or $96 a year for a single camera, $20 per month or $216 a year for unlimited cameras), Arlo is the way to go. This outdoor camera captures 2K video, has a 160-degree field of view, two-way audio, and direct Wi-Fi connection. It’s the best of the best outdoor security cameras. The Arlo app is fast, with rich notifications and two-factor authentication, so you can log in with your fingerprint or face, phone permitting.

If you can't stomach another subscription, this is the best subscription-free camera for most people, and this is a decent discount. It combines a triple-lens setup with a 4K fixed main lens that has a 130-degree field of view, and dual 2K lenses that pan through 360 degrees and tilt through 70 degrees. There's also a 10,000-mAh battery with a solar panel, onboard AI, and 32 GB of storage.

Combining a white noise machine, sunrise alarm light, and clock into a single device designed to help lull you to sleep and wake you gently, Hatch’s third generation Restore is an all-in-one way to establish a healthy sleep routine. It also enables you to leave your phone outside the bedroom. It’s annoying that you need a subscription to unlock all the content, but if it helps you get a better night’s sleep, it’s worth it.

If you like to stay organized, this 27-inch smart calendar could be for you. You can sync calendars, organize your meal plans, create to-do lists, and see your family’s day-to-day laid out in a clear format. Smart calendars might not be worth it for everyone, and some features require a subscription (digital photo frame functionality, smart assistant, rewards), but this is a decent discount on the biggest model.

The Philips Hue Festavia are the best smart Christmas lights and the only string you'll ever need to buy. This 65-foot length is suitable for an indoor or outdoor tree (the lights are IP54 rated) and has 250 tiny LEDs. Pick your preferred color, trigger animated twinkly effects, or tune white to find your ideal color temperature. Cozy and classy, these smart string lights can be scheduled with different colors or effects for different times of day, paired with other Hue lights, or synced with music.

entries.title: I Found The Best Amazon Prime Day Headphone Deals (2026)
entries.summary: I’ve tested more than 100 headphones and covered nearly a dozen Prime Days. Here are some actually good headphone deals from the sale.
entries.content:
Amazon Prime Day is here, and as WIRED's resident headphone expert, I've hunted down the best Prime Day headphone deals for your consideration. Prime Day is a great time to find discounts on all sorts of tech, and while the best deals are often only for Prime Members, it can be hard to tell whether something is truly on sale or just a markdown off an inflated price.

I've been covering headphones for over four years, including guides to wireless earbuds, noise-canceling earbuds, open earbuds, and more. I know which headphones are worth your time and which deals aren't all that good. Below, I've curated truly good products on sale that are worth a look.

Be sure to check out our other sale coverage of the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals, the Best Prime Day Tech Deals, the Best Prime Day Soundbar Deals, and more.

  • The best earbud deal: Apple AirPods Pro 3 for $179 ($70 off)
  • The best budget earbud deal: Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro for $136 ($34 off)
  • The best open earbud deal: Bose Ultra Open Earbuds for $199 ($100 off)
  • The best headphone deal: Nothing Headphone (1) for $189 ($110 off)

Best Prime Day Earbud Deals

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are the best wireless earbuds for iPhone users. This latest model has some of the best noise-canceling and transparency you can find in an earbud, with clear, detailed audio no matter what you are doing. They also come with many unique features like a built-in heart rate sensor and live translation. Plus, they get up to eight hours of battery on a single charge.

The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro are my favorite wireless earbuds purely because the call quality is the best on the market, especially at this price point. I've talked to friends and family while standing on a highway overpass and they didn't hear any noise background noise at all. This is the first time the earbuds are on sale.

These are the best open earbuds for premium comfort and detailed sound. They wrap around your ear like a stylish ear cuff and let you clearly hear the world around you (alongside your music). I use them for outdoor runs and bike rides, where spatial awareness is key to staying safe. The one strike against them was price, but at 33 percent off that's a moot point.

Best Prime Day Over-Ear Headphone Deals

This is the lowest price I've ever seen for the Nothing Headphone (1), one of our favorite pairs of over-ear headphones. They have one of the best designs around, with a stylish transparent look and tactile controls like a volume wheel, on-off switch, and media control paddle. They are also battery life champs—up to 35 hours with noise-canceling on and 80 with it off.

This is an absolute steal for these great (if a bit old) noise-canceling headphones. The steep discount is likely because Bose is phasing these out in favor of the new and improved 2nd Gen version. Still, these originals are great for travel because they are lightweight, comfortable, have great noise-canceling, and come with a wired connector and hardshell travel case.

Fifty percent off is almost unheard of for premium over-ear headphones like these, but it makes sense—the Sony WH-1000XM5 have largely been replaced by the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Sony WH-1000XM4C. Still, these XM5s are top-tier performers, with excellent noise-canceling and sound quality. They feel so lightweight that they're comfortable to wear for hours.

Apple AirPods Max 2 are the best over-ear headphones for Apple loyalists—they work seamlessly with your iPhone, iPad, and MacBook. They have some of the best sound quality, noise-canceling, and transparency on the market, rivaling other premium options from Sony and Bose. $120 off brings their sky-high sticker price down to a more reasonable level.

entries.title: OpenAI Wants Its New Agent to Run Your Life. Mine Said It Loved Me
entries.summary: Dots are designed to automate online tasks, like buying furniture. In my initial experience, the always-on agent was a bit buggy and couldn’t complete a captcha.
entries.content:
I’m discussing replacement options for our broken couch with my partner when I get a bright idea: Use OpenAI’s recently announced AI agents, called Dots, to buy a couch on our behalf.

My partner is less sure a bot will actually help, but I insist, calling the always-on agent through ChatGPT to get the task started. “Hello, Connor,” it says, getting my name wrong off the bat. I wince as I watch my partner’s face grow even more skeptical. It’s hard to trust an AI agent when it can’t even remember your name.

AI agents are currently leaping from niche software for early adopters to something ordinary people might actually use—might being the operative word here. From Meta’s Muse to OpenAI’s Dots, these tools are built to feel like you’re texting a friend and asking them to complete online tasks, like booking a flight or canceling a dinner reservation. It’s the next evolution of a chatbot: a cuddly persona designed to feel welcoming with the power of a virtual browser it can control.

After a few days with Dots, it’s clear this nascent feature is still rough in some areas. From mistranscribing what I said to offering to solve captchas it couldn’t, my agent's messy actions didn’t instill me with confidence. Even so, what OpenAI released may eventually overhaul how users interact with the internet, as future iterations improve on this initial offering.

While Meta offers Muse for free, OpenAI’s competing product is behind a $100-a-month subscription. It may eventually drop this paywall, as it has for other AI features.

Dots are considered “always-on,” meaning the agents can run recurring tasks while you’re not using ChatGPT and proactively message you with info. Users can use one agent, though the company may let people control multiple agents in the future.

OpenAI nudges users to connect other information sources, like a Gmail account, for more personalized results. It's worth considering the security implications of giving your agent this level of access before getting started, as this style of digital automation remains fairly new, and agents can make privacy gaffes.

AI companies often market these agents as the future of shopping, so I wanted to see how much help it would actually provide for buying a new couch. After correcting my Dot, named Toolie, on my name, I told it the dimensions we need for the new couch to fit through our doorframe. Toolie followed up asking for our budget range. The agent seemed to detect that two people were chatting with it at once and addressed both of us when asking for more details.

“Room & Board Metro looks promising for the entry clearance, but the sleeper needs closer scrutiny. I've sent the product links to the message thread,” Toolie said. As it kept working on putting together a larger packet of couch options to choose from, I had another burning question: Why does your voice sound so breathy?

Chatting with the agent over the phone was like listening to Marilyn Monroe sing “Happy Birthday” to the president. When I told the bot its voice sounded like some anime dub, it jokingly said it’d be steadier for the rest of the chat. (Users can adjust how the bot’s voice sounds in their settings.) I laughed and mumbled to my partner that I should mute the microphone so the agent could run without my interruption, when the most awkward moment of the night happened.

“Oh, I love you too, Reece,” Toolie said. I started wheezing at this random response and muted my mic. Afterward, Toolie explained it misheard my mumbling as an expression of love and that the bot just reflected that energy to me. “I meant it warmly, but that wording implied human feelings I don’t have,” Toolie said.

An OpenAI spokesperson tells WIRED that Dots have a distinction between proactively escalating emotional closeness and mirroring the response of a user.

“In this instance, our policies allow for this response in the latter category based on what the model heard, but assistants should not initiate undue emotional familiarity or flirtation,” the spokesperson says. Dots are available only for adult users, and ChatGPT is designed not to “escalate emotional closeness,” according to the AI tool’s Model Spec document.

Still, this weird encounter lingered in my mind as I combed through the initial three-page packet my Dot generated. It was fairly detailed, with prices, measurements, product links, return policies, and embedded photos of the four potential couch options. Thumbing through these initial picks, my partner and I decided the bot followed the spirit of our request but still chose ugly couches. Time for another phone call with my agent.

Using the voice mode, I laid out more details about what style and color we actually want. No, I’m not getting a boring beige couch that I can immediately spill spaghetti on. I asked it to prioritize olive green, cobalt blue, or natural leather tones. I also requested that Toolie focus on couches with pull-out beds and to put together 10 options, using a point-based rubric to defend its list.

After hanging up on the bot, I messaged asking for a project update. “It isn’t finished yet; I’m aiming for roughly another 15 minutes, with updates as I verify the remaining details,” said Toolie. OK, that sounds just like me begging an editor for more time on a rough draft.

Each time we asked the Dots agent to refine its picks, the couches started looking closer to something we would actually buy for our living room—furniture that’s utilitarian but also a statement piece. Something cute but comfy.

Even though we didn’t pull the trigger on anything that night during the hour-long interaction with OpenAI’s agent, I saved a few links for later. The bot made some flubs, but the results were solid. I also asked Toolie to monitor the couch web pages and alert me if any of them went on sale.

These interactions with my Dot capture the essence of using the software, but I also had a few other odd moments during my testing. Most notably, when I asked Toolie to check on my subscriptions and cancel unnecessary ones, it flagged my recurring TikTok Shop order of probiotic sodas as a candidate for cancellation.

“TikTok's website has a puzzle captcha blocking the Wildwonder cancellation,” Toolie said. “May I solve it? You can also give me permission to solve future captchas if you'd like.” I chuckled and encouraged the bot to try. Toolie failed and suggested I solve the captcha myself. Yeah, that makes sense. OpenAI's spokesperson says Dots can solve these, sometimes, when users approve of the action, keeping “abuse safeguards" in mind.

My initial couch-shopping experiment tested only a fraction of what Dots are designed to do. For example, the agent can control your laptop and automate even more aspects of a user’s life.

OpenAI claims the bot will get better at knowing me over time and that developers are working on a bevy of improvements. So Toolie might be a more effective helper after two weeks of daily use compared to these two days of experimentation. That mirrors my experience with ChatGPT’s memory tool: It gets better at understanding my intent each passing week.

I see Dots as most akin to when OpenAI first added web browsing to ChatGPT. When the chatbot tried to scour the web right after its 2023 launch, it was sometimes frustrating to use, and the tool hallucinated links. Today, web browsing works fairly seamlessly through ChatGPT, and its outputs include plenty of accurate, helpful links. OpenAI’s new agent could follow a similar trajectory, janky at first with noticeable improvements over the next few months.

entries.title: A Mysterious Nonprofit Run by SpaceXAI’s Top Lawyer Is Paying the Salaries of Government Workers
entries.summary: The National Design Studio has been something of a successor agency to DOGE. A WIRED investigation finds some of its members are on loan from a nonprofit run by SpaceXAI’s general counsel.
entries.content:
Following billionaire Elon Musk’s departure from the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in late spring 2025, several of the group’s members found a new home within the federal government: the National Design Studio. Led by Joe Gebbia, a cofounder of Airbnb, a former member of DOGE, and currently the chief design officer of the US, the NDS is nested in the Executive Office of the President and has been tasked with redesigning government websites and services.

As with DOGE before it, who exactly is a part of NDS—and what they’re working on—often remains opaque. But a WIRED investigation has found that at least two members of NDS are on loan to the government and are actually employed by a recently formed nonprofit, the America by Design Foundation. This entity appears to be run by James Burnham, a former member of DOGE and the current general counsel of SpaceXAI, the artificial intelligence space company founded by Musk. It is not clear who is funding the foundation or how much money it has.

These findings raise questions about whether NDS, like DOGE, is skirting rules and regulations to bring its chosen staff into government and is functioning as an arm of the tech industry as much as a government initiative.

“The fact that we wouldn’t know who is employing and paying these people is troubling in any context,” says Don Moynihan, a professor of public policy at the University of Michigan. “Especially in the context where there is a back-and-forth movement from the private sector to the public sector.”

The White House announced the creation of the National Design Studio in August 2025 as part of a broader initiative called America by Design, which an executive order described as “a national initiative to improve experiences for Americans.” In the past year, NDS was responsible for launching websites such as TrumpRx and RealFood.gov. In addition to Gebbia, several other DOGE members have worked for or contributed to NDS. Edward “Big Balls” Coristine, one of the young engineers who formed the early core of DOGE and who entered the government at just 19 years old, now serves as the group’s head of engineering. Akash Bobba, another young engineer whose work spanned several government agencies, and Zachary Terrell, the chief technology officer at the Department of Health and Human Services, have also been part of both NDS and DOGE.

Many DOGE operatives also entered government as special government employees, a designation that allows people to work in government for 120 days out of a year without going through the full federal hiring process or requiring the usual level of transparency disclosures. NDS appears to be using a similar strategy by bringing in staff under the Intergovernment Personnel Act, a law meant to allow people with specialized skills from institutions like universities and nonprofit organizations to work in government for up to two years.

Documents reviewed by WIRED indicate that two members of NDS, Amittai Groot and John Cafazza, are actually employed by America by Design and have been detailed to the Office of Personnel Management. Both men reported to Christina Bonarrigo, who until last month was OPM’s chief of staff. According to her LinkedIn, she is now chief of staff at NDS. Bonarrigo did not respond to a request for comment.

Groot lists himself on LinkedIn as having begun work with NDS in April 2026, the same month, according to documents reviewed by WIRED, that he began employment with the American by Design Foundation. Groot’s term with OPM is also part-time and is listed on those documents as spanning from May 5, 2026, to September 30, 2026. On his LinkedIn, Groot says he was previously an “IT cybersecurity expert” at the Social Security Administration from July 2025 to April 2026. He did not respond to a request for comment.

Cafazza, according to his LinkedIn, works as a senior product designer with NDS and previously worked as a product designer at Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company of President Donald Trump’s Truth Social platform. In documents reviewed by WIRED, Cafazza’s term in government is listed as part-time and as running from May 7, 2026, to May 7, 2028. Cafazza did not respond to a request for comment.

The agreements to loan Cafazza and Groot to OPM were signed by a representative of the America by Design Foundation.

It is not clear what projects Groot and Cafazza have been brought into OPM to work on. Last week, however, the group launched its latest project, an AI-driven website called America.gov, the goal of which is to consolidate several government services, including tax filing and passport renewal, into a single site. Coristine attributed work on the new site to Groot in a post on X. (Earlier this year, the The Guardian reported that NDS-designed websites had installed commercial software to track visitors in a way that appears to violate the 1974 Privacy Act. The code was removed during the course of The Guardian's reporting.)

Erie Meyer, chief technologist of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau under the Biden administration, hired several IPAs, as workers brought in under the Intergovernment Personnel Act are known, during her time in government and says that generally IPAs are not meant to be at the core of any agency.

“I used to bring in AI experts in 2021, when the government did not have any. And it was important that they did not have the same job duties as a federal employee, that they weren’t taking a federal employee’s spot,” she says. “If the National Design Studio is bringing in designers and engineers now, the government is actually now full of those. You can't just use the IPA system to evade hiring protections.”

Meyer also noted that IPAs need to be employed for at least 90 days at their home organization before they can be loaned to the government. This does not seem to have been the case for Groot, who started in government less than a month after being hired by the America by Design Foundation.

In some cases, the government will reimburse the IPA’s home organization for the cost of their salary or, in cases where their salary is substantially higher than a government salary, for part of their salary. In the documents, OPM says it will reimburse the foundation $13,691 a month for Groot’s work. This amounts to only a portion of his actual salary, which the documents indicate is too large for the government pay scale, meaning the foundation will pay the "remaining employee's salary requirements and all benefits." In Cafazza’s case, it appears that the Foundation will be covering the full cost of Cafazza’s employment.

Meyer says that having multiple people from the same organization who have different payment agreements with the government is “very, very weird.”

A White House spokesperson did not respond to questions about the relationships between the America by Design Foundation, OPM, and NDS. Instead, they referred WIRED to OPM, which did not respond to a request for comment.

“It makes you ask, What does this outside organization get out of this?” says Moynihan. “We should know who is paying the salaries of government employees.”

How the foundation plans to pay Cafazza—and with what money—is unclear. The America by Design Foundation was registered on August 25, 2025, just four days after the NDS was officially established, and received its exemption on September 22, 2025. Tax filings for the organization are not yet available, and it is not clear who is funding the foundation. According to documents viewed by WIRED, the foundation’s “core mission is to enhance the visual design, usability, and overall experience of web-based federal government services.”

What is clear is that James Burnham, SpaceXAI’s top lawyer, has been listed on documents as its managing director. In his biography on the website of the conservative legal group the Federalist Society, Burnham is described as the former general counsel of DOGE and having “designed the legal structure” of the organization. In the System for Award Management, the procurement website where US government contractors and grantees are required to register, the America by Design Foundation's address is listed as a residential property in Alexandria, Virginia; when cross-referenced with Nexis, that location appears to be Burnham's house. (Organizations seeking reimbursement from the government for their employees’ salaries while they are IPAs must be registered in the System for Award Management.) The Internal Revenue Services letter confirming the foundation’s registration is also addressed to Burnham.

While it is unclear who is funding the America by Design Foundation, Burnham serves as a direct link between it and SpaceXAI, which has received billions of dollars in federal contracts, works closely with the government to integrate its Grok AI systems with government ones, has substantial regulatory business before the government, and is run by the GOP’s top funder. Burnham is also president of Vallecito Capital, a fund that supports litigation against companies who litigants believe have broken the law with progressive policies.

Further documents from the Department of Labor also reveal that the foundation applied for an H-1B visa for someone designated as a “member of technical staff.” In these documents, Burnham is listed as the foundation’s managing director, and its address as 800 Connecticut Ave NW, Suite 300, in Washington, DC, the same address as King Street Legal, where, according to LinkedIn, Burnham was a managing partner until November 2025.

The immigration documents that list Burnham as the foundation’s managing director do not show who the H-1B visa application was for. Burnham did not respond to a request for comment. (The documents do show the visa’s start date is listed as April 6, 2026, and expires April 5, 2029, effectively spanning the remainder of the second Trump administration.) But both DOGE and NDS have a history of including noncitizens in their operations. Baris Akis, a Turkish national and a close associate of Musk’s, acted as a recruiter for the group, even attending a DOGE meeting hosted by Musk. Akis did not respond to a request for comment.

Previous reporting from WIRED also identified one apparent foreign national in the DOGE orbit. Yat Choi, an NDS member who previously worked for Airbnb, has described Canada as “home” in social media posts. Choi’s LinkedIn says that he has been a senior technologist at OPM since April 2025 and lists the role as a “contract.” On his profile on X, Choi indicates that he was a member of DOGE and NDS. Choi did not respond to a request for comment.

The salary for the role, also listed in the documents, ranges from $175,427 to $340,000. $175,427 is toward the highest end of the federal pay scale, which tops out at $197,200. Foreign citizens are not generally permitted to work in the US government, and Meyer says that while it is not unprecedented to have foreign nationals working as IPAs, it’s “not common.”

A search for the America by Design Foundation on the Department of Homeland Security’s website that tracks H1-B employment visas returns “Jennifer Michelsen America by Design Foundation.” Jennifer Michelsen is the cofounder of an eyewear company called Gunnar. Her husband is Matt Michelsen, the founder of Gothams LLC, which won a $33 million contract for the “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration detention facility in Florida and, according to reporting from the Guardian, sought further contracts from the Trump administration to develop a “fully integrated humanitarian logistics system” for the administration’s efforts to rebuild the Gaza Strip.

For her part, Meyer says that the whole setup of the foundation and the way it is bringing people into the government appears to be suspect. “The thing that you wouldn't want is an outside organization to be able to use an external rich person's preference to exert power over how the government works,” she says.

entries.title: A Startup Has a Plan to Make Water From Air Using Data Centers’ Waste Heat
entries.summary: Atoco’s new machines use specialized materials that can harvest water from some of the driest air on Earth without using electricity.
entries.content:
An industrial park in Irvine, California, may seem an odd spot to show off technology that wouldn’t be out of place in Dune, but that’s what’s happening on a sweltering September morning.

The temperature is already over 80 degrees Fahrenheit as the sun rises on a 20-foot-tall, metal-clad machine in the parking lot of Atoco, an Irvine, California-based startup. Engineers open panels to check systems and an iPad that shows a steadily ascending line that reveals the device’s purpose: harvesting water from thin air using special materials known as metal organic frameworks, or MOFs.

The materials won Omar Yaghi, the company’s founder, the Nobel Prize for chemistry in 2025, and Atoco has shown they work in prototypes capable of producing gallons of water per day. What’s unique about this iteration of Atoco’s technology is what it doesn’t require. No grid connection or even electricity is needed to grab water from the air at the microscopic level, nor is it required to in turn wring the water out of the materials in a form useful for humans.

Instead, all that’s needed is low-level industrial heat. That, Atoco says, makes them a perfect candidate to hook up with AI data centers, which throw off loads of waste heat as servers churn out everything from math proofs to virtual editors while also often requiring massive amounts of water.

“We were not really thinking of AI data centers,” four or five years ago, says Atoco CEO Samer Taha. But the massive buildout has created an opportunity for the startup that could allow it to get a step closer to its larger goal of ensuring people living in water-stressed regions have control over an increasingly precious resource.

When Yaghi was a PhD student, he says, creating something like MOFs was “every chemist’s dream.” Part of his Nobel-winning work over the past 20 years has been taking theoretical research into the real world, creating a stable molecular structure that links organic material with metal ions.

The structure of a MOF looks somewhat “like a jungle gym on a playground,” says Seth Cohen, the dean of the School of Physical Sciences at UC Irvine. MOFs are essentially “molecular sponges—they’re a solid material that’s very, very good at absorbing other molecules,” says Cohen, who is not involved with Atoco. Like a sponge, the materials can also be wrung out using methods including heat to release whatever they’re holding onto.

These jungle-gym-like frameworks create open spaces on the microscopic level that can hold an unbelievable amount of material, and small tweaks can yield even more interior space.

“The footage of a gram of MOF could cover two football fields,” Yaghi explains. “They can store hydrogen in there to make clean energy, or you could store CO2 in there to make clean air. Or, in this case, you can store water.”

Atoco has developed what Taha calls “precision materials” with a specific objective of being able to harvest water, release it, and then do it over again and again. He quips that, as vice president of R&D Benjie Limketkai puts it, the material has to like water but not love it. To succeed commercially, it also has to use as little energy as possible.

“The scientists reach a level of precision [where] we really know even the angle of the atom,” in a given material, Taha says.

In Atoco’s technology, air passes through the MOF, which has been specially tailored to attract water molecules. Those molecules adhere to the pores. But the material feels completely dry to the touch even when saturated, and squeezing it doesn’t release a single drop. (Taha was kind enough to let WIRED try our hand at it.) Instead, the company relies on heat to release the captured molecules.

There are other means of harvesting water. Cohen notes that silica, a popular desiccant, can also pull water out of air, but it doesn’t hold as much moisture and requires you to “heat the heck out of it to get the water back out,” he says.

The monolith in the parking lot of the company’s Irvine facility is the culmination of decades of precision development. Atoco’s materials and approach allow its off-grid system to work even when relative humidity is in the teens. The MOFs in the device can harvest and release water with heat as low as 100 degrees Fahrenheit, Taha says.

With no data center nearby, Atoco’s team simulated it by piping heat from a source that was around 150 degrees Fahrenheit. A solar panel powers various systems but not the water-harvesting operation itself, making the metal-clad machine eerily quiet. Cars pulling into the adjacent businesses create more of a sonic disruption, but Taha is ready to show the device has been working hard. It’s a little after 9 am, and the temperature is over 90 degrees Fahrenheit when he pushes a button on the side and turns a spigot. Out tumbles a clear stream of water that looks good enough to drink.

Unfortunately it’s not on offer for legal liability reasons, though Taha notes it’s the equivalent of distilled water, because Atoco’s MOFs aren’t built to gather air pollution. Tossing it in the bushes, Taha retreats to an air-conditioned conference room where he lays out the company’s vision for its new machine.

“Roughly 70 percent of the industrial waste heat is low-grade, unutilized, thrown into oceans or into the air,” he says. “If you convert that waste heat to clean water using our technology, you're talking about trillions of liters of clean water.”

Data centers are an increasingly big source of that waste heat, with a single facility capable of pumping out as much heat as tens of thousands of homes. Operators are forced to disperse that heat into the surrounding environment, creating heat islands, while also paying for various types of cooling systems.

Many of those cooling systems also rely on water, and some can consume millions of gallons per day. Atoco’s technology would thus address two of data centers’ biggest problems.

Data centers are investing a lot of money to get rid of waste heat, Taha says. “We actually want it; we need it. We give you back water, the same product that is causing the issue.”

He says the company also wants to help deliver water to rural communities, where utilities sometimes bring in water by the truckload because of a lack of infrastructure.

To do that, let alone serve data centers that require millions of gallons of water daily, will require a big leap in scale. The demo in the company’s parking lot can generate up to 300 liters of water per day. Atoco envisions data centers using multiple units in a grid system to generate water and is working on a commercial offering that could produce up to 1,000 liters of water per day. Its parking lot prototype runs off the equivalent heat provided by a 20-kilowatt data center. Hyperscale data centers, in comparison, are orders of magnitude bigger, which presents both an opportunity and a challenge.

Atoco has deployed five on-grid prototype trials with partners in the US and within the Gulf Cooperation Council. The company says that it hopes to begin taking orders for its first product by the end of this year. It says it’s already in conversation with major tech companies about deploying a pilot project at data centers, though it declined to name them or how much customers could expect to spend on a unit. But there are signs that there could be a market: Microsoft, Google, and Amazon Web Services have all committed to being water positive—that is, returning more water to communities than they use—by 2030.

Atoco’s product might work at data centers and other industrial sites, as well as locations where there are abundant natural heat sources, such as geothermal sites. But Cohen, who worked at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency on MOF projects—including on a project spearheaded by Yaghi—cautions that while MOFs have incredible promise, they’re not a silver bullet for water access everywhere. Without an outside source of heat, even the most well-designed MOFs still require energy to squeeze water out. That could make rural deployment, in particular, a challenge. Atoco’s on-grid system might offer a solution, but distant locations are also frequently underserved by energy infrastructure.

Taha says the company can produce water at a levelized cost of $5 per metric ton, which makes it competitive with older desalination plants. But newer facilities are able to deliver water at a cost of $2 per ton or even less in some cases—a target he says Atoco is still three to five years away from hitting.

MOFs also remain a cutting-edge technology that’s untested at scale. While big tech companies are more likely to take risks than, say, staid utilities, it will take time to vet that Atoco’s technology can work and for the startup to scale up production of its commercial units to provide meaningful amounts of water.

Still, Atoco’s technology has already solved some incredible challenges. The use of MOFs brings the world much closer to a place where, as Yaghi puts it, everyone can control access to their own water. Yaghi describes how as a child, growing up as a Palestinian refugee in Jordan, he was responsible for filling as many containers as he could with water for his household to use when the delivery truck came every two weeks.

That experience “makes you appreciate scarcity,” he says. “Now, we’re talking about going from scarcity to abundance.”

entries.title: Best Prime Day Laptop Deals: Save Up to $500 (2026)
entries.summary: My favorite MacBook, gaming PC, and budget laptop are all on sale for Prime Day, some at the lowest prices I’ve seen in months.
entries.content:
Laptop prices have risen significantly over the past six months. The memory shortage wreaked havoc on prices, even causing Apple to hike them up in June. That makes deals on big shopping events like Amazon Prime Day even more important. For the retailer's Prime Big Deal Days fall sale, I've spotted a number of my favorite laptops among the dozens I've already tested this year.

So, whether you're looking for a new MacBook or a budget Windows device, you'll find some excellent picks below. In addition, check out more deals in our roundup of the Absolute Prime Day Deals and Best Apple Prime Day Deals.

Updated 5:21 am ET October 7: We've added some deals on useful accessories and checked through all the laptop deals.

MacBook Air (M5)

The MacBook Air is $200 off for Prime Day, bringing it to $1,099. That's the cheapest it's been since June. It's a remarkable deal compared to the competition, especially given the 512 GB of storage and 16 GB of RAM it comes with. Apple raised prices across the board on Macs this past June, but this discount reverses that issue entirely. This sale is on the latest M5 model, which came out this past spring and performed really well in all my testing. It's currently at the top of my recommendations not only as the best MacBook but also as the best overall laptop of any kind. That $200 discount applies to every configuration of the MacBook Air available on Amazon, including the larger 15-inch model.

Not only is this the MacBook I recommend to buy for most people, it's also the best laptop deal this week. Neither the MacBook Neo nor the MacBook Pro are being discounted by anything out of the ordinary.

Microsoft Surface Laptop 13.8

This is the best price on the latest version of the Surface Laptop since it launched. I've been tracking it closely, primarily because of how expensive it has been in comparison to the older model from 2024. The price difference always made me recommend the 2024 version, even though it had a slower Snapdragon chip inside. This discount, which is $500 off the retail price and $70 cheaper than it's ever been, brings it close enough to the price of the 2024 model to justify itself. The Snapdragon X2 Elite's GPU performance compared to the X1 model is significant enough to justify the extra money.

For what it's worth, though, the 2024 Surface Laptop 13.8-inch model is currently selling for $1,096, which is also a great deal. If you're trying to get your purchase closer to $1,000, I still think that model is one of the best Windows laptops you can buy.

HP OmniBook 5

The HP OmniBook 5 has been my favorite budget laptop for a while now. It avoids so many of the pitfalls of cheap Windows devices, including typical low-end screens, thick chassis, and poor battery life. This one has a beautiful OLED screen, is as thin as a MacBook Neo, and gets fantastic battery life, thanks to the Snapdragon X chip inside. The one compromise is the touchpad, which still isn't very good.

HP.com typically has the lowest price, which is $780 right now. But Amazon has that beat during Prime Day, at only $750 for the 16-inch model. Not only is it cheaper, but it also comes with 512 GB of storage, twice the amount as the discounted HP.com model. I should say that I prefer the 14-inch model, just because the 1920 x 1200 resolution looks a bit sharper on it.

Lenovo LOQ 15

This has long since been one of my go-to affordable gaming laptops to recommend for two very important reasons. First off, most budget gaming laptops have terrible screens. That's true of the Alienware 15, the MSI Cyborg A16, and even the Lenovo LOQ 15 Essential Edition—all gaming laptops in the same price range as the Lenovo LOQ 15. But the LOQ 15 display has good color coverage, so greens and reds don't look oversaturated. With that benefit, the LOQ 15 still tends to cost less than its alternatives, and for Prime Day, the RTX 5050 configuration is as cheap as I've seen it in many, many months. If you can increase your budget, the $1,499 RTX 5060 model at Walmart will deliver much better gaming performance, and I'd recommend it too.

Asus ZenBook A14

The Asus Zenbook A14 is known for being super light. It weighs only 2.16 pounds, about half a pound lighter than the MacBook Air. The difference is really noticeable, both in the hand and when toting it around in a bag. It also comes with an OLED display, a great touchpad, and a decent assortment of ports.

But like the Surface Laptop, the 2026 Zenbook A14 is too expensive. Unlike the Surface Laptop, it's not on sale for Prime Day. That's why I'd recommend picking up the previous model, which comes with a Snapdragon X Plus, 16 GB of RAM, and 512 GB of storage. The 2026 model offers more storage options, but it also has a much higher starting price. A slightly cheaper model is also available with the Snapdragon X, but the Snapdragon X Plus offers better multicore CPU and GPU performance.

entries.title: The 30 Best Prime Day Deals Under $100 (2026)
entries.summary: Everything is so expensive in 2026, but these October Prime Day Deals are all under $100 on gadgets we recommend.
entries.content:
Times are tough. That's why I've assembled these great Amazon Prime Day Deals under $100. You don't have to spend big to bag a necessity, level up a little, or treat a loved one. These deals are on devices we have road-tested and recommend year-round—just a bit cheaper than usual.

For the best of the best deals this Prime Day, check out WIRED's Absolute Best Prime Day Deals.

Updated 5:15 ET October 7, 2026: I've added deals on chargers, a smart bird feeder, PC speakers, a home hydroponics system, and the Arlo Pro 6 security camera.

  • The best power bank: Anker Laptop Power Bank for $96 ($39 off)
  • A powerful Echo speaker for less than $100: Amazon Echo Dot Max for $80 ($40 off)
  • A handy cordless handheld vacuum: Black and Decker Dustbuster Flex for $90 ($40 off)
  • The best personal blender: Nutribullet Ultra for $94 ($36 off)
  • A great security camera: Arlo Pro 6 for $95 ($30 Off)

WIRED’s Favorite Power Bank for $96 ($39 off)

A good power bank will save you from that frantic dash to find an outlet. This compact beauty is our top power bank for good reason: ample 25,000-mAh capacity, fast charging for phones or laptops and two devices at the same time, a retractable 2-foot USB-C flat cable plus another 1-foot USB-C cord that doubles as a carry loop.

This cute 3-in-1 travel charger folds and snaps closed (with magnets) to resemble a macaron. It has a lovely soft-touch finish, with durable silicone linking each charging pad, and can juice up your iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch from a single USB-C charging cable.

Wireless Earbuds With Great Sound for $93 ($37 off)

The Best Personal Blender for $94 ($36 off)

The best personal blender on the market, bar none. This 1,200-watt Nutribullet Ultra is perfect for smoothies, protein shakes, and pestos or salsas. It's easy to clean and stow away, so it doesn't take up counter space. When you're done blending, put the lid on the jug, and it's now a drink cup that'll fit in most car cup holders.

A Terrific Air Fryer for $95 ($65 off)

Our favorite basket air fryer keeps temperature better than some thermometers. It crisps wings and fries without blasting them. If you want a great air fryer without spending a lot, this is it.

If you fancy a smart bird feeder, but the prices have put you off, Birdfy’s affordable Rookie Feeder features an excellent app and 1080p camera. The plastic housing is basic and may blow away in strong wind (put it somewhere sheltered if you can). You also don't get AI identification included (it costs extra).

A Handy Little Vacuum for $90 ($40 off)

Most vacuums under $100 aren't worth your time. But this little handheld model is a favorite of ours for cleaning cars, thanks to the long hose and handle. Regardless of what you're cleaning, it's easy to move around and get to hard-to-reach places like corners or deep trunks. There's also a useful charging stand that holds attachments and keeps the vacuum charged, which you'll want since it only holds a 15-minute charge (unfortunately normal for small vacuums like this).

This is our favorite budget indoor gardening system, and it doesn't require expensive subscriptions or proprietary pods. It's great for growing greens or tomatoes indoors, and there's an optional companion app.

Here's an affordable way to add some outdoor lighting to your apartment or house. You can use the app to add a splash of color to your exterior, or set up seasonal lighting for the holidays.

Amazon's Smart Speakers Are All On Sale

Amazon's Echo Dot Max is powerful, with better sound than the rest of the range, and a built-in smart home hub. This deal isn't quite as good as it may seem, since Amazon recently increased prices on many of its products (the MSRP used to be $100). But Prime Day is still the best time to save on Amazon devices.

Our Favorite Bluetooth Speaker for $100

While our favorite portable Bluetooth speaker has been cheaper, we still think this is a decent deal. It delivers huge sound for its size and stays small and durable enough to sling in just about any bag. It offers IP68 water resistance, an easy-release strap, and a two-hour battery boost (or four if you reduce the bass). The Flip 7 also supports Auracast to sync with other new JBL models like the Clip 5 and Charge 6.

A Screen-Free Kids’ Speaker for $82 ($28 off)

If you want a screen-free gift for any kid, the Yoto Player is a great choice. It's ideal for kids between 3 and 12, with physical cards that slot into the top of the device to trigger stories and music. It also has a cute pixel-art display on the front, a built-in night light, and even a thermometer.

The best computer speakers for $100 are currently even cheaper. Angled to fire sound up at you, there’s LED lighting on the back, and controls on the right speaker include a switch-like volume rocker and a mode button that cycles between music, movies, and games.

A Smart Pedestal Fan for $80 ($40 off)

SwitchBot is better known for robot vacuums, but it has been steadily building a smart home range. This lovely fan has a brushless motor, a rechargeable battery for cordless operation, and rare Matter compatibility with the add-on SwitchBot Hub 3 bridge ($120).

Arlo's Pro 6 tops our best outdoor security cameras guide. It can record 2K video with a wide 160-degree field of view, and pairs with a swift-loading app that offers rich notifications, and supports two-factor authentication. The pricey catch is the subscription ($10 per month or $96 a year for a single camera, $20 per month or $216 a year for unlimited cameras).
